artifacts.summary: Codebase research on verify-deploy.sh/run-all.sh gate-framework refactor: confirms Gate 8's unanchored-grep defect and 4 sibling occurrences, finds the dispatch's contended cost figures (542s shellcheck, straggler invocation count, six-gate cost table) do not reproduce on an idle re-measurement, surfaces an unaccounted-for 124s Gate 3 cost, and identifies run-all.sh's existing scheduler and manifest-routing-lib.sh as direct reusable prior art for the declarative gate registry.

memory_candidates.content: In agent-system/extensions/core, a cost figure for a verify-deploy.sh gate or lint script measured in the same session as other heavy concurrent process activity can be wrong in EITHER direction relative to a clean idle re-measurement, not just inflated -- observed both a 7x-too-high figure (lint-shellcheck.sh: 542s contended vs 75.9s idle) and several moderately-too-low figures (lint-scoped-commit-boundary.sh, lint-directory-pathspec-boundary.sh, lint-task-lookup-adoption.sh: idle measurements 1.65-1.76x SLOWER than the contended figures cited). Always re-measure idle (uptime load < 2) via --only-gate before using a cost figure to prioritize optimization work.

shellcheck (v0.11.0) has no internal --jobs/parallel flag. Naive xargs -P batched-file parallelization (multiple files per shellcheck invocation, several invocations concurrent) measured SLOWER than sequential at every tested batch size (-P24-n20, -P4-n96, -P8-n48) on a 24-core host -- only true one-process-per-file dispatch (-P24-n1) beat sequential, and only by ~1.5x, not an order of magnitude. Likely cause: per-process memory/GC contention from many concurrent Haskell-runtime processes, not CPU starvation (user CPU time summed to 8-9 minutes across shapes while wall time barely improved or regressed). Any future shellcheck parallelization in this codebase must use one-process-per-file dispatch and must re-verify the speedup empirically rather than assuming linear core-count scaling.

agent-system/extensions/core/scripts/lib/manifest-routing-lib.sh is a proven precedent in this codebase for a declarative-registry pattern: data declared in a structured file (manifest.json's routing_agents), consumed by one shared sourced library implementing a precedence ladder, validated by its own dedicated lint (lint-routing-wiring.sh) and test (test-routing-resolution.sh). Use this as the structural model whenever a future task needs to replace copy-pasted per-item logic (e.g. verify-deploy.sh's 23 copy-pasted gate blocks) with a data-driven registry, rather than inventing a new JSON schema and runner from scratch.
